title: Student notes: the Kessra sky survey
bodyMd:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes.

- The Kessra sky survey was a project to photograph the entire southern night sky on glass plates.
- The survey was begun in 1911 at the Mount Orrin observatory.
- Its last plate, the 9,400th, was exposed in 1958.
- The plates are now stored in a climate-controlled archive in Valparaíso, Chile.
- In 2021, a team led by astronomer Tomás Ibarra began scanning the plates.
- Comparing the old plates with modern images lets astronomers find stars whose brightness has changed over the past century.
accessibilityText: A list of six research notes taken by a student about the Kessra sky survey. One: the survey was a project to photograph the entire southern night sky on glass plates. Two: it was begun in 1911 at the Mount Orrin observatory. Three: its last plate, the 9,400th, was exposed in 1958. Four: the plates are now stored in a climate-controlled archive in Valparaíso, Chile. Five: in 2021, a team led by astronomer Tomás Ibarra began scanning the plates. Six: comparing the old plates with modern images lets astronomers find stars whose brightness has changed over the past century.

provenance.notes: Original note set written for this item bank. The Kessra survey, the Mount Orrin observatory, the archive and Tomás Ibarra are invented; photographic plate surveys are described only in general terms and no source was adapted.
